name: Today's Report
headline: Rates are flat for a third straight session at 6.89%, while Canada's new counter tariffs put 50% on steel and aluminum and 25% on appliances, which lands squarely in remodel budgets.
teaser: Mortgage rates did not move again. Mortgage News Daily has the 30-year at 6.89% and the 15-year at 6.49%, both unchanged on Tuesday, which makes three sessions running at the same level. The 10-Year Treasury drifted up to 4.80%, so if anything the pressure is gently upward from here.

sections.label: Real estate
sections.html:
Mortgage rates did not move again. Mortgage News Daily has the 30-year at 6.89% and the 15-year at 6.49%, both unchanged on Tuesday, which makes three sessions running at the same level. The 10-Year Treasury drifted up to 4.80%, so if anything the pressure is gently upward from here.

The story worth your attention has nothing to do with rates. Canada's counter tariffs took effect yesterday, and the rates land on things that go into houses: 50% on steel and aluminum, 25% on appliances like washers and dryers, 15% on machinery parts and air conditioners.

  • Read the chart below carefully, because the tidy version circulating today is misleading. These are rate tiers, not category rates. Canada set each product's rate to mirror the matching U.S. tariff on the same good, so one everyday category straddles tiers: an air conditioner is taxed at 15% while a washing machine is taxed at 25%.
  • Direction matters too. These are Canadian tariffs on goods going north, so the direct hit is to U.S. exporters. What reaches a Bay Area remodel is the second order effect, through cross border supply chains and steel pricing that is already at records.
  • One number to correct: the order covers C$27.6 billion of imports, Canadian dollars. Reported as an unmarked "$27.6B" it reads as U.S. dollars to an American audience. At today's exchange rate it is about US$20 billion, so the unmarked figure overstates the scope by roughly 38%.

Alameda County (Fremont Focus)

  • Board wide: 2,640 listings across our 15 city table, counting active and in contract together, with 220 coming soon and 144 brand new.
  • Five city ledger: 698 live listings across Fremont, Hayward, Milpitas, Newark and Union City. 598 are already on the market and 100 are coming soon.
  • Fremont: 267 live, 207 active, 41 coming soon, 19 brand new. The median on market list price is $1,218,444 at $823 a square foot, and the typical active listing has been out 27 days.
  • The rest of the ledger: Hayward 186, Milpitas 114, Newark 77, Union City 54.
  • Across all five cities the median is $1,075,485 at $694 a square foot. 276 homes are priced under a million, and 159 have been sitting 60 days or longer.

What this means for you: inventory keeps climbing, from 695 live listings yesterday to 698 today, with 82 arriving in the past week. That is the third straight day of growth and it is genuinely good news if you have been losing out on offers. On the selling side the arithmetic is getting harder to ignore: 159 of the 598 homes on the market, better than one in four, have now been waiting two months or more. Add tariffs to appliance and steel costs and a renovation you were planning before listing gets more expensive, which is an argument for pricing right the first time rather than remodeling your way to a higher number.

images.source: Source: Department of Finance Canada, list of U.S. products subject to counter-tariffs effective September 8, 2026. The order covers C$27.6 billion of imports, about US$20 billion.

sections.label: Economy
sections.html:
Gold gave back 1.7% on Tuesday to close near $4,400 an ounce, its sharpest drop in over a week, while silver held up better at a little over $66. Brent settled at $97.92, up 1.7%, and is trading above $100 this morning. The 10-Year crept up to 4.80%, the highest close in more than a week.

The survey behind today's second chart is a genuinely interesting read on how new technology actually gets adopted. McKinsey asked 5,500 farmers across 10 countries about AI, and 17% now use generative AI in farm work, making it the fastest spreading technology in agriculture. The catch is in the split: of that 17%, about 12 points are people using free versions and only 4 points are paying for a tool.

The more interesting number is trust. Just 6% of farmers treat an AI chatbot as a trusted input when deciding what to buy. That sounds dismissive until you see it was 1% in 2024, which makes it the fastest growing purchasing input in the whole survey. For scale, web search sits at 18% and social media at 9%. Trust is being earned quickly, from almost nothing.

It is a useful mirror for any business, including this one. People will try a new tool enthusiastically, use the free version indefinitely, and take considerably longer before they let it influence a decision that costs money.

A note on the newsletter's numbers, because two did not hold up. It put the 10-Year at 4.79% and up 0.01, while Treasury's own daily curve shows 4.80% against Friday's 4.78%, a move of 0.02. It also had Brent at $99.27 against the ICE front month settlement of $97.92. Gold at $4,401 was right this time, and silver was left out again, so we sourced it ourselves.

images.alt: Chart of a McKinsey survey of 5,500 farmers in 10 countries: 17% use generative AI, split into 12% using only free versions and 4% paying, and 6% trust AI for buying decisions, up from 1% in 2024, against web search at 18% and social media at 9%.
images.caption: Of the 17% of farmers using generative AI, roughly 12 points use only free versions and 4 points pay. Trust for purchasing is small at 6%, but it was 1% in 2024.
images.source: Source: McKinsey Global Farmer Insights 2026, published September 8, 2026, fielded April to June 2026. The free and paid shares sum to 16% against a 17% total; the difference is rounding in the source.

sections.label: Stocks
sections.html:
Tuesday was a broad step back, with the Dow taking the worst of it at more than a percent. As of 9:21 AM PT this morning the slide has continued: the S&P is near 7,628, the Dow near 52,328 and the Nasdaq near 26,212, all below Tuesday's close. Those are live intraday quotes and will move before the bell.

Apple is expected to unveil its first foldable iPhone today, a passport sized device with a 7.8 inch inner screen, priced well above the $799 base model and reportedly targeting 7 to 10 million units. Huawei and Xiaomi launched foldables of their own on Monday.

Two deals worth noting. Qualcomm is teaming with Amazon to put its chips in AWS data centers, granting Amazon the right to buy 25 million shares at $161.26, roughly $4 billion if exercised. And GE Aerospace is buying its parts supplier Consolidated Precision Products for $11.75 billion, betting demand for a key engine part jumps more than 30% by 2030.

sections.label: Crypto
sections.html:
Live quotes pulled at 9:21 AM PT with 24 hour changes. All three are close to flat, with Bitcoin hovering near $78,500 for a third day and XRP the weakest of the group. After two days of correcting this section, credit where due: the newsletter's crypto levels were accurate today.

Visa is pushing further into stablecoin cards, which let you spend dollar pegged crypto like cash. Visa already runs more than 160 such programs and wants to share payment data so crypto lenders can underwrite the companies behind those cards faster.

Robinhood is going bigger on prediction markets, taking stakes in Crypto.com and OG.com and routing its prediction trades through OG.com's U.S. exchange. Worth watching rather than acting on: several states are moving to ban prediction markets over consumer protection concerns, so the regulatory ground here is not settled.
